content: The Pneumococcal Vaccine 13-Valent is a vaccine approved by the FDA for the prevention of infections caused by specific Streptococcus pneumoniae serotypes. It is indicated for use in children aged 6 weeks to 17 years and adults aged 50 years and older. The vaccine is administered intramuscularly as a single dose in adults and as a four-dose series in infants at 2, 4, 6, and 12–15 months of age. For children aged 7 months to 5 years who have not received the vaccine, a catch-up schedule is recommended, though it may result in lower antibody concentrations for some serotypes compared to the standard four-dose series. It must not be used if it cannot be resuspended or if particulate matter or discoloration is observed. It should not be mixed with other vaccines or products in the same syringe. The preferred injection sites are the anterolateral aspect of the thigh in infants and the deltoid muscle of the upper arm in toddlers, children, and adults. Injection into the gluteal area or areas near major nerve trunks or blood vessels should be avoided. Common adverse reactions include redness, swelling, and pain at the injection site, as well as systemic reactions such as fatigue, headache, decreased appetite, and muscle or joint pain. In clinical trials, serious adverse events were reported in a small percentage of recipients, with no significant differences between the 13-valent and 7-valent pneumococcal vaccines. Rarely, apnea has been observed in premature infants following intramuscular vaccination, and decisions regarding vaccination in this population should consider the infant's medical status and the potential benefits and risks. Contraindications include severe allergic reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis) to any component of the vaccine or to any diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine. Epinephrine and other agents for managing immediate allergic reactions should be readily available in case of an acute anaphylactic reaction. The safety of the vaccine has been evaluated in multiple clinical trials involving thousands of infants, children, and adults. Solicited local and systemic adverse reactions were monitored using electronic diaries, and serious adverse events were collected throughout the study periods. The most commonly reported serious adverse events in infants and toddlers included infections such as bronchiolitis, gastroenteritis, and pneumonia. Deaths reported in clinical trials were consistent with background rates for the population studied and were not directly attributed to the vaccine. Postmarketing surveillance has identified additional adverse events, including administration site conditions and systemic reactions. However, due to the voluntary nature of these reports, it is not always possible to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to the vaccine.
